Injured in a Savannah Car Accident? Get the Compensation You Deserve.

A car accident in Savannah can change everything in an instant — mounting medical bills, lost income, and pain that disrupts every part of your life. At Roden Law, our car accident lawyers have recovered more than $300 million for injured clients across Georgia and South Carolina, and our Savannah team is ready to fight for the full compensation you deserve. There are no upfront fees and no costs unless we win your case. If you or a loved one has been hurt in a Savannah car accident, call (912) 303-5850 today for a free, no-obligation consultation.

Why Savannah Car Accidents Are Uniquely Dangerous

Savannah's roads present a combination of hazards that make serious car accidents far too common in Chatham County. The city sits at a critical transportation crossroads, and the factors that make Savannah a thriving coastal city also make its roadways some of the most dangerous in Georgia.

The I-16 and I-95 interchange west of the city is one of the highest-volume junctions in the Southeast. Thousands of long-haul trucks and passenger vehicles merge through this corridor daily, and the mix of high-speed interstate traffic with vehicles entering and exiting creates a persistent collision risk. Accidents at this interchange frequently involve commercial vehicles, including tractor-trailers traveling to and from the Port of Savannah — the busiest single-terminal container port in North America. The sheer volume of truck traffic in Savannah contributes to more severe crashes involving catastrophic injuries and wrongful death.

Within the city, Abercorn Street and Truman Parkway are two of the most accident-prone corridors. Abercorn Street runs through heavily commercial areas with frequent turning movements, congested shopping centers, and pedestrian activity. Truman Parkway, while designed as a limited-access route, sees dangerous speed differentials and merging conflicts, particularly during rush hour.

Savannah's role as a major tourist destination adds another layer of risk. The Historic District draws millions of visitors each year who are unfamiliar with the city's distinctive square-based street grid, leading to unpredictable driving behavior at intersections. During the spring and summer months, traffic to Tybee Island along U.S. Route 80 creates seasonal congestion spikes that lead to rear-end collisions and intersection crashes. From the interstate corridors to the downtown squares, Savannah drivers face dangers that demand experienced legal representation when accidents occur.

Common Causes of Car Accidents in Savannah

Understanding what caused your crash is essential to building a strong injury claim. Our Savannah car accident attorneys investigate every case thoroughly and see certain patterns repeated across Chatham County collisions:

  • Distracted driving — Texting, phone use, and in-car distractions remain the leading cause of preventable crashes in Savannah, particularly along congested commercial corridors like Abercorn Street and Montgomery Cross Road.
  • Speeding — Excessive speed on Truman Parkway, DeRenne Avenue, and I-516 reduces reaction time and dramatically increases the severity of injuries in a collision.
  • Drunk driving — Savannah's open-container laws and active nightlife along River Street and City Market contribute to a higher-than-average rate of DUI-related crashes, particularly on weekend evenings.
  • Failure to yield and red-light running — Dangerous intersections such as Victory Drive and Abercorn Street, DeRenne Avenue and Abercorn Street, and the Oglethorpe Mall area see frequent T-bone collisions caused by drivers who ignore traffic signals.
  • Rear-end collisions — Stop-and-go traffic on Abercorn Street and during Tybee Island beach traffic on U.S. 80 leads to frequent rear-end crashes that can cause serious neck and back injuries.
  • Weather-related accidents — Coastal fog, sudden afternoon thunderstorms, and standing water on low-lying roads throughout Chatham County create hazardous driving conditions that catch motorists off guard.
  • Hit-and-run accidents — Savannah sees a significant number of hit-and-run crashes each year, leaving victims to navigate complex insurance claims without knowing who struck them.

Types of Car Accident Injuries We Handle

Car accidents in Savannah range from minor fender-benders to devastating high-speed collisions that leave victims with life-altering injuries. Roden Law represents clients suffering from the full spectrum of car accident injuries, including:

  • Whiplash and soft tissue injuries — Even low-speed collisions can cause neck and back injuries that result in chronic pain and long recovery periods.
  • Traumatic brain injuries (TBI) — Concussions and more severe brain injuries can cause cognitive impairment, memory loss, and permanent disability.
  • Spinal cord injuries — Herniated discs, fractured vertebrae, and spinal cord damage can result in partial or complete paralysis.
  • Broken bones and fractures — High-impact collisions frequently cause fractures to the arms, legs, ribs, pelvis, and facial bones that may require surgical repair.
  • Internal bleeding and organ damage — Blunt force trauma from a car accident can cause life-threatening internal injuries that may not be immediately apparent.
  • Burns and lacerations — Vehicle fires, airbag deployment, and broken glass can cause scarring and disfigurement.

When a Savannah car accident results in the death of a loved one, our Savannah wrongful death lawyers help families pursue justice and financial security through a wrongful death claim under Georgia law.

Georgia Car Accident Laws That Affect Your Case

Georgia law governs every aspect of a car accident claim filed in Savannah, from filing deadlines to how fault is determined. Understanding these laws is critical to protecting your right to compensation.

Statute of Limitations — Two Years to File

Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, you have two years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit in Georgia. If a loved one was killed in the crash, the wrongful death statute of limitations is also two years under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. Missing this deadline almost always means losing your right to recover compensation entirely, regardless of how strong your case may be. While two years may seem like adequate time, building a strong case requires prompt investigation, and critical evidence can be lost or destroyed in the weeks after a crash.

Georgia's Modified Comparative Fault Rule

Georgia follows a modified comparative fault system under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33. This means you can recover compensation as long as you are less than 50 percent at fault for the accident. However, your total compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault. For example, if you are awarded $200,000 but found 20 percent at fault, your recovery would be reduced to $160,000. If you are 50 percent or more at fault, you recover nothing. Insurance companies routinely try to shift blame onto accident victims to reduce or eliminate payouts, which is why having an experienced attorney who can counter these tactics is essential.

Georgia's Mandatory Auto Insurance Minimums

Under O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11, Georgia requires all drivers to carry minimum liability insurance of $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident for bodily injury and $25,000 for property damage (commonly referred to as 25/50/25 coverage). These minimums are often insufficient to cover the cost of serious injuries. When the at-fault driver's insurance is inadequate, our attorneys explore every available avenue of recovery, including underinsured motorist (UIM) claims and third-party liability claims against employers, vehicle manufacturers, or government entities responsible for road conditions.

Georgia Is an At-Fault Insurance State

Georgia operates under an at-fault insurance system, meaning the driver who caused the accident is financially responsible for the other party's injuries and damages. Injured victims in Savannah can pursue compensation by filing a claim with the at-fault driver's insurance company, filing a claim with their own insurance under uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage, or filing a personal injury lawsuit in Chatham County Superior Court. Most car accident claims are resolved through insurance negotiations, but Roden Law prepares every case as if it will go to trial, which gives our clients significant leverage during settlement discussions.

What to Do After a Car Accident in Savannah

The actions you take in the hours and days following a car accident can significantly impact the outcome of your claim. If you have been involved in a crash in Savannah or anywhere in Chatham County, follow these steps to protect your health and your legal rights:

  • Call 911 immediately. Georgia law requires you to report any accident involving injuries, death, or property damage exceeding $500. A Savannah-Chatham Metropolitan Police Department report creates an official record of the crash.
  • Seek medical attention right away. Even if you feel fine at the scene, many serious injuries — including traumatic brain injuries and internal bleeding — have delayed symptoms. Visit a Savannah-area emergency room or urgent care facility and keep all records of your treatment.
  • Document the scene. If you are physically able, take photos and video of vehicle damage, road conditions, traffic signals, skid marks, and any visible injuries. Collect names and contact information from witnesses.
  • Do not admit fault. Anything you say at the scene or to an insurance adjuster can be used against you. Limit your statements to the facts and avoid apologizing or speculating about what happened.
  • Do not accept a quick insurance settlement. Insurance companies often contact accident victims within days of a crash with lowball offers designed to close the claim before the full extent of injuries is known.
  • Contact a Savannah car accident attorney. Call Roden Law at (912) 303-5850 before speaking with the other driver's insurance company. Our attorneys handle all communication and negotiation so you can focus on recovery.

Injured in a car accident in Savannah? Time is critical. Call Roden Law at (912) 303-5850 or contact us online for a free case review. There is no fee unless we recover compensation for you.

How Roden Law Fights for Savannah Car Accident Victims

When you hire Roden Law to handle your Savannah car accident case, you get a legal team that knows how to build claims that maximize compensation. Our approach begins with a thorough independent investigation — our attorneys do not rely solely on police reports. The team works to obtain surveillance camera footage, black box data, cell phone records, and any other evidence that establishes liability before it can be lost or destroyed.

Roden Law retains accident reconstruction experts, medical specialists, and economists who can testify about the cause of the crash, the full extent of your injuries, and the long-term financial impact on your life. This expert testimony strengthens your case during negotiations and at trial.

Our attorneys are aggressive negotiators, but what sets Roden Law apart is a genuine willingness to take cases to trial when insurance companies refuse to offer fair compensation. Insurance adjusters know which firms actually try cases — and that reputation directly benefits our clients during settlement discussions. Attorney Eric Roden and the Savannah team at our office located at 333 Commercial Dr., Savannah, GA 31406 are committed to achieving the best possible result for every client.

Compensation You May Recover After a Savannah Car Accident

Georgia law allows car accident victims to seek compensation for the full range of losses caused by another driver's negligence. Depending on the circumstances of your case, you may be entitled to recover:

  • Medical expenses — Emergency room visits, surgery, hospitalization, physical therapy, prescription medications, and all future medical care related to your injuries.
  • Lost wages and earning capacity — Compensation for income lost during recovery, as well as diminished future earning capacity if your injuries prevent you from returning to your previous occupation.
  • Pain and suffering — Damages for physical pain, emotional distress, anxiety, depression, and reduced quality of life resulting from the accident.
  • Property damage — Repair or replacement costs for your vehicle and any personal property damaged in the crash.
  • Loss of consortium — Compensation available to spouses for the loss of companionship and support caused by a serious injury.
  • Punitive damages — In cases involving egregious conduct such as drunk driving accidents, Georgia courts may award punitive damages under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1 to punish the at-fault driver and deter similar behavior.

Every car accident case is different, and the value of your claim depends on factors including the severity of your injuries, the available insurance coverage, and the strength of the evidence. Roden Law evaluates each case individually and fights to recover every dollar our clients are owed.

Why Choose Roden Law for Your Savannah Car Accident Case

Choosing the right attorney after a car accident is one of the most important decisions you will make. Roden Law offers Savannah accident victims a powerful combination of resources, experience, and commitment:

  • $300 million+ recovered for injured clients across Georgia and South Carolina.
  • 5,000+ cases handled — extensive experience with car accident claims of all types, from rideshare accidents to multi-vehicle interstate collisions.
  • No fee unless we win — every car accident case is handled on a contingency fee basis, meaning you pay nothing out of pocket and owe no attorney fees unless Roden Law recovers compensation for you.
  • Licensed in Georgia and South Carolina — our attorneys handle claims across both states, serving clients from five office locations.
  • Local Savannah presence — our Savannah office is staffed with attorneys and support staff who know Chatham County roads, courts, and insurance practices.
  • Motorcycle accidents, truck crashes, and complex claims — Roden Law handles the full range of motor vehicle accident cases in Savannah, not just standard car collisions.

Talk to a Savannah Car Accident Lawyer Today

If you have been injured in a car accident in Savannah, Chatham County, or anywhere in Southeast Georgia, do not wait to get legal help. Georgia's two-year statute of limitations means critical evidence and legal deadlines can slip away faster than you expect. Our downtown office sits at 127 King Street, Suite 200, minutes from the Charleston County courthouse. Call (843) 790-8999 for a free, confidential case review.

Why Choose Roden Law for a Charleston Car Accident Claim

Charleston's peninsula geography and heavy tourist traffic make its crashes uniquely complex, and the local insurance defense bar knows it. What sets Roden Law apart is direct attorney involvement: you work with your attorney — not a rotating desk of case managers — from intake through settlement or verdict. Our King Street office is steps from the Charleston County Court of Common Pleas, so filings, hearings, and client meetings happen without delay.

  • No fee unless we win — free consultation and no upfront cost to start your claim.
  • Local Lowcountry knowledge — we know the peninsula corridors, the bridges, and the out-of-state-driver dynamics that drive Charleston crashes.
  • Trial-ready — we build every car accident case as if it will be tried, which is what moves insurers to pay full value.

Common Causes of Charleston Car Accidents

The collisions our Charleston attorneys handle most often involve:

  • Bridge and crosstown crashes on the Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge to Mount Pleasant and the US-17 Crosstown (Septima P. Clark Parkway).
  • Interstate merge and rear-end collisions on the I-26 and I-526 corridors, including the high-crash I-26/I-526 interchange.
  • Tourist-district and rideshare crashes around the King and Market Street grid, where out-of-state drivers, carriage tours, and rideshare drop-offs mix.
  • Pedestrian and bicycle collisions in the dense downtown peninsula and on Savannah Highway (US-17).
  • Uninsured and underinsured drivers — a frequent problem in claims that exceed South Carolina's 25/50/25 minimum policy limits.

South Carolina Car Accident Law: What Charleston Drivers Need to Know

You Have 3 Years to File

South Carolina's statute of limitations for car accident injury claims is three years from the date of the crash under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. If a government entity such as SCDOT or the City of Charleston is a defendant, a much shorter Tort Claims Act deadline applies — two years from discovery (S.C. Code § 15-78-110) — another reason to talk to an attorney early.

The 51% Comparative-Fault Bar

South Carolina uses modified comparative fault: you can recover as long as you are less than 51% responsible, with your award reduced by your share of fault. Insurers routinely try to shift blame onto you — our attorneys anticipate and dismantle that tactic.

Stacking UM/UIM Coverage

When an at-fault driver carries only minimum limits, South Carolina lets you stack uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage across policies. On a serious bridge or interstate crash, stacked UM/UIM is frequently the largest available source of recovery.

Compensation in a Charleston Car Accident Case

  • Medical expenses — ambulance, ER, surgery, hospitalization, rehabilitation, and future care.
  • Lost wages and lost earning capacity — for time off work and any permanent limitation on your ability to earn.
  • Pain and suffering — non-economic damages, which South Carolina does not cap in standard car accident cases.
  • Property damage — repair or replacement of your vehicle.
  • Punitive damages — available where the at-fault driver's conduct was reckless, such as drunk or extreme-speed driving.

Your Charleston Crash Checklist

  1. Call 911 and get a police report — Charleston PD, the county sheriff, or SC Highway Patrol depending on where the crash occurred.
  2. Photograph the vehicles, the scene, road conditions, and any visible injuries before anything is moved.
  3. Collect the other driver's insurance information and witness names and numbers.
  4. Seek medical care promptly — serious injuries from a bridge or interstate crash are often not obvious at the scene, and treatment gaps are used against you. Critical patients are routed to MUSC Health, the Lowcountry's only Level I trauma center.
  5. Do not give a recorded statement to the at-fault insurer before speaking with an attorney.
  6. Call Roden Law's Charleston office at (843) 790-8999 for a free case evaluation.

Columbia's car accident market is crowded with high-volume advertising firms. Our office at 1545 Sumter Street, Suite B sits in the downtown corridor minutes from the Richland County Court of Common Pleas, so filings, hearings, and client meetings happen without the delays that come from running a Midlands case out of a distant Charleston or Atlanta office.

  • No fee unless we win — free consultation and no out-of-pocket cost to start your claim.

  • Trial-ready — we build every car accident case as if it will be tried, which is what moves insurers to pay full value.

Common Causes of Columbia Car Accidents

Three interstates converge in the Midlands, and the resulting through-traffic drives the region's most serious collisions. The crashes our Columbia attorneys handle most often involve:

  • Distracted and rear-end collisions on the I-20/I-26/I-77 "Malfunction Junction" interchange and its active Carolina Crossroads work zones.
  • Intersection and left-turn crashes along Two Notch Road (US-1), Garners Ferry Road, Forest Drive, and Broad River Road.
  • DUI and late-night crashes in the USC and Five Points entertainment district, especially on weekends.
  • Commercial truck and distribution-center traffic feeding the I-77 and I-20 corridors.
  • Uninsured and underinsured drivers — a frequent problem in claims that exceed South Carolina's 25/50/25 minimum policy limits.

South Carolina Car Accident Law: What Columbia Drivers Need to Know

You Have 3 Years to File

South Carolina's statute of limitations for car accident injury claims is three years from the date of the crash under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. Waiting is still costly — skid marks fade, vehicles are repaired or scrapped, and witness memories blur. The sooner we investigate, the stronger your claim.

The 51% Comparative-Fault Bar

South Carolina uses modified comparative fault: you can recover as long as you are less than 51% responsible, with your award reduced by your share of fault. Insurers routinely try to push blame onto you to cut their payout — our attorneys anticipate and dismantle that tactic.

Stacking UM/UIM Coverage

When an at-fault driver carries only minimum limits, South Carolina lets you stack uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage across policies. On a serious Malfunction Junction pile-up, stacked UM/UIM is frequently the largest available source of recovery — and the one insurers are least eager to explain.

Compensation in a Columbia Car Accident Case

  • Medical expenses — ambulance, ER, surgery, hospitalization, rehabilitation, and future care.
  • Lost wages and lost earning capacity — for time off work and any permanent limitation on your ability to earn.
  • Pain and suffering — non-economic damages, which South Carolina does not cap in standard car accident cases.
  • Property damage — repair or replacement of your vehicle.
  • Punitive damages — available where the at-fault driver's conduct was reckless, such as drunk or extreme-speed driving.

Your Columbia Crash Checklist

  1. Call 911 and get a police report — Columbia PD, Richland County Sheriff, or SC Highway Patrol depending on where the crash occurred.
  2. Photograph the vehicles, the scene, road conditions, and any visible injuries before anything is moved.
  3. Collect the other driver's insurance information and the names and numbers of any witnesses.
  4. Seek medical care promptly — serious injuries from a Midlands highway crash are often not obvious at the scene, and gaps in treatment are used against you.
  5. Do not give a recorded statement to the at-fault insurer before speaking with an attorney.
  6. Call Roden Law's Columbia office at (803) 219-2816 for a free case evaluation.

posts.post_title: Truck Accident Lawyers in Savannah, GA
posts.post_content:
Savannah Truck Accident Lawyers — Aggressive Advocacy After Catastrophic Collisions

Savannah sits at the crossroads of two of the Southeast's busiest freight corridors, and the consequences are measured in shattered lives. When a fully loaded tractor-trailer weighing up to 80,000 pounds collides with a passenger vehicle, the injuries are rarely minor — they are catastrophic, life-altering, and often fatal.

Roden Law has recovered more than $300 million for injured clients across Georgia and South Carolina. The Savannah office team understands the unique trucking dangers facing Chatham County residents, and the firm brings the resources, investigative depth, and trial willingness needed to hold negligent trucking companies accountable.

If you or a family member has been injured in a truck accident in Savannah or surrounding Southeast Georgia, call (912) 303-5850 for a free consultation. Roden Law handles every truck accident case on a contingency fee basis — there are no attorney fees unless the case is won.

Why Savannah Is a Truck Accident Hotspot

Savannah is not just a historic coastal city — it is one of the most active freight hubs in the United States. The Port of Savannah, operated by the Georgia Ports Authority, is the busiest single-terminal container port in North America and the third-busiest port in the country overall. Every year, millions of container units move through the port and onto Georgia's highways aboard thousands of tractor-trailers.

The consequences for local roadways are significant. Interstate 16 connects Savannah to Macon and Atlanta, functioning as a primary east-west freight artery that channels port traffic deep into the state. Interstate 95, the major north-south corridor along the Eastern Seaboard, passes directly through Chatham County. Together, these two interstates funnel an estimated 15,000 or more commercial trucks per day through the Savannah metropolitan area.

Beyond the interstates, secondary roads bear a heavy burden as well. Jimmy DeLoach Parkway serves as a direct connector between the port and I-95, carrying a concentrated stream of container trucks through the rapidly developing Pooler industrial corridor. Warehousing and distribution centers along this stretch continue to expand, adding more truck traffic to roads that were not originally designed for such volume.

Seasonal patterns make the danger worse. Holiday freight surges in the fall and winter dramatically increase truck volume, while agricultural shipments from South Georgia — including Vidalia onions, pecans, and timber — add heavy loads to I-16 during harvest months. These peaks coincide with higher passenger vehicle traffic, creating a dangerous combination on already congested highways. For Savannah residents, the risk of a serious truck collision is not abstract — it is a daily reality of living in one of America's busiest port cities.

Who Is Liable in a Savannah Truck Accident?

Truck accident cases are fundamentally different from standard car accident claims in Savannah because multiple parties may share legal responsibility. Identifying every liable party is critical to maximizing the compensation available to injured victims.

The Truck Driver

Driver negligence remains the most common cause of truck accidents. This includes fatigued driving in violation of federal Hours of Service regulations, distracted driving, driving under the influence, speeding, and aggressive lane changes. When a driver violates federal safety rules, that violation can serve as powerful evidence of negligence.

The Trucking Company

Under the legal doctrine of respondeat superior, a trucking company is liable for the negligent acts of its drivers committed within the scope of employment. Beyond vicarious liability, trucking companies can be held directly liable for negligent hiring, training, retention, and supervision. Companies that fail to screen drivers for poor safety records, skip required drug and alcohol testing, or pressure drivers to exceed legal driving hours bear direct responsibility for the crashes that result.

Cargo Loading Companies

Third-party companies responsible for loading freight can be liable when overloaded or improperly secured cargo causes a truck to become unstable, shift during transit, or spill onto the roadway. Federal regulations set strict weight limits and securement standards — violations create liability.

Vehicle and Parts Manufacturers

When a mechanical defect causes or contributes to a crash, the manufacturer of the truck or the defective component may be liable under Georgia product liability law. Brake failures, tire blowouts, defective coupling devices, and steering system malfunctions are among the most common equipment-related causes of truck accidents.

The Role of Federal Regulations

The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) enforces comprehensive safety regulations under 49 CFR Parts 390 through 399 that govern nearly every aspect of commercial trucking. Violations of these regulations — whether related to driver qualifications, vehicle maintenance, cargo securement, or hours of service — are not merely administrative infractions. In a Georgia courtroom, FMCSA violations serve as compelling evidence that a trucking company or driver failed to meet the minimum standard of care required by law.

Common Types of Truck Accidents in Savannah

The size, weight, and configuration of commercial trucks create accident patterns that are distinct from passenger vehicle collisions. Roden Law's truck accident attorneys handle every type of commercial vehicle crash, including:

  • Jackknife accidents — The trailer swings outward at an acute angle to the cab, often sweeping across multiple lanes of traffic on I-16 or I-95.
  • Underride and override accidents — A passenger vehicle slides beneath the trailer of a truck, frequently resulting in fatal or catastrophic head and neck injuries.
  • Wide-turn accidents — Trucks making right turns swing into adjacent lanes, crushing vehicles alongside them, particularly at Savannah's downtown intersections.
  • Rear-end collisions — A loaded truck traveling at highway speed requires up to 40 percent more stopping distance than a passenger vehicle, making rear-end crashes devastatingly forceful.
  • Blind spot accidents — Commercial trucks have massive blind spots along both sides, the front, and the rear. Lane-change collisions on I-95 are a frequent result.
  • Rollover accidents — Hazardous materials trucks and tanker trucks are especially vulnerable to rollovers on curved highway ramps and exit lanes.
  • 18-wheeler and semi-truck collisions — The most common type of catastrophic truck accident, involving the largest and heaviest vehicles on the road.

Georgia Truck Accident Laws

Truck accident claims in Savannah are governed by Georgia state law as well as federal trucking regulations. Understanding both legal frameworks is essential to building a successful case.

Statute of Limitations

Under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, Georgia imposes a two-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims arising from truck accidents. The clock begins running on the date of the accident. If a victim dies from truck accident injuries, the wrongful death statute of limitations is also two years from the date of death under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. Failing to file a lawsuit within this window forfeits the right to seek compensation entirely. Given the complexity of truck accident investigations, contacting an attorney promptly is critical.

Georgia's Modified Comparative Fault Rule

Georgia follows a modified comparative fault system under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33. An injured person can recover damages only if their own percentage of fault is less than 50 percent. If the injured person is found to be 50 percent or more at fault, recovery is barred completely. When fault is below that threshold, the damages award is reduced by the plaintiff's percentage of fault. Trucking companies and their insurers routinely attempt to shift blame onto the injured motorist — experienced legal representation is essential to defeating these tactics.

Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations

The FMCSA's regulations under 49 CFR Parts 390 through 399 establish mandatory safety standards for the commercial trucking industry. Key regulations that frequently arise in Savannah truck accident cases include:

  • Hours of Service (HOS) rules (49 CFR Part 395) — Drivers of property-carrying vehicles may drive a maximum of 11 hours after 10 consecutive hours off duty, within a 14-hour on-duty window. Violations of these limits are a leading cause of fatigue-related truck accidents.
  • Electronic Logging Device (ELD) mandate — Since 2017, most commercial trucks are required to use ELDs to electronically record driving hours, replacing paper logbooks that were easily falsified.
  • Vehicle maintenance and inspection standards (49 CFR Parts 393 and 396) — Trucking companies must conduct regular inspections, maintain detailed maintenance records, and ensure vehicles meet minimum safety standards before operating on public roads.
  • Driver qualification standards (49 CFR Part 391) — Requirements for medical fitness, driving history review, drug and alcohol testing, and commercial driver's license qualifications.

Evidence Preservation

Truck accident evidence is perishable. Electronic control module (ECM) data — commonly called the truck's "black box" — records speed, braking, and engine performance in the moments before a crash but may be overwritten within days. Driver logs, ELD data, GPS records, dash cam footage, weigh station reports, and vehicle maintenance records are all subject to routine destruction under company retention policies. Sending a spoliation letter demanding preservation of this evidence is one of the first and most critical steps in any truck accident case.

Filing in Chatham County

Truck accident lawsuits arising from crashes in the Savannah area are typically filed in Chatham County Superior Court. Roden Law's attorneys regularly practice in this court and understand the local procedures, judges, and litigation dynamics that affect case strategy and outcomes.

Truck Accident Injuries Are More Severe

The sheer physics of a collision between an 80,000-pound commercial truck and a 4,000-pound passenger vehicle produce injuries that are dramatically more severe than those in typical motor vehicle accidents. Truck accident victims in Savannah frequently suffer:

  • Traumatic brain injuries (TBI) — Ranging from concussions to severe diffuse axonal injuries that cause permanent cognitive impairment.
  • Spinal cord injuries and paralysis — Complete or incomplete spinal cord damage resulting in paraplegia or quadriplegia, requiring lifelong medical care.
  • Amputations and crush injuries — The force of a truck collision can destroy limbs beyond surgical repair.
  • Severe burn injuries — Particularly in accidents involving fuel tank ruptures, hazardous materials, or post-collision fires.
  • Multiple fractures and internal organ damage — Broken bones, ruptured organs, and internal bleeding requiring emergency surgery and extended hospitalization.
  • Wrongful death — Truck accidents are disproportionately fatal. Surviving family members may pursue wrongful death claims under Georgia law.

The medical costs associated with these injuries are staggering. A single traumatic brain injury can generate millions of dollars in lifetime treatment, rehabilitation, and lost earning capacity. Roden Law works with medical experts, life care planners, and vocational economists to ensure that every component of a client's damages is fully documented and aggressively pursued.

How Roden Law Investigates Truck Accident Cases

Truck accident cases demand an investigative approach that goes far beyond what is required in a standard motor vehicle crash. The Savannah truck accident attorneys at Roden Law deploy a comprehensive investigation strategy designed to uncover every source of liability and every piece of available evidence.

Rapid Evidence Preservation

Within 24 hours of taking a case, Roden Law sends formal spoliation preservation letters to the trucking company, its insurer, and all related parties demanding that they preserve all evidence related to the crash. This includes ECM/black box data, ELD records, driver qualification files, dispatch communications, GPS and telematics data, dash cam and trailer camera footage, drug and alcohol testing records, and vehicle inspection and maintenance logs.

Accident Reconstruction

Roden Law retains independent accident reconstruction experts who analyze physical evidence from the crash scene, vehicle damage patterns, electronic data, and witness testimony to establish exactly how the accident occurred and who was at fault. In cases involving complex multi-vehicle crashes on I-16 or I-95, this expert analysis is often the most important evidence presented at trial.

FMCSA Compliance Audit

The legal team conducts a thorough review of the trucking company's compliance history, including its FMCSA Safety Measurement System (SMS) scores, prior inspection results, out-of-service violations, and any history of enforcement actions. A trucking company with a pattern of safety violations is far more vulnerable to claims of negligent operation — and that history is a matter of public record that Roden Law knows how to access and use effectively.

Building the Full Picture

Additional evidence sources include weigh station records from Georgia Department of Public Safety inspection stations, toll records, fuel purchase receipts that establish the driver's route and timeline, and employment records that reveal whether the company was pushing drivers beyond legal limits. Every detail matters, and overlooking a single source of evidence can mean leaving significant compensation on the table.

Compensation Available in Savannah Truck Accident Cases

Because of the severity of injuries involved, truck accident claims typically involve substantially higher damages than standard motor vehicle accident cases. Roden Law pursues the full range of compensation available under Georgia law, including:

  • Medical expenses — Past, present, and future costs of hospitalization, surgery, rehabilitation, medication, and ongoing care.
  • Lost wages and lost earning capacity — Compensation for income lost during recovery and for diminished ability to earn in the future.
  • Pain and suffering — Physical pain, emotional distress, and diminished quality of life resulting from the injuries.
  • Disability and disfigurement — Compensation for permanent impairments, scarring, and loss of bodily function.
  • Loss of consortium — Damages available to the spouse of a seriously injured victim for loss of companionship and support.
  • Wrongful death damages — Full value of the life of the deceased, including future earning capacity, and funeral and burial expenses.
  • Punitive damages — In cases involving willful misconduct, fraud, or conscious disregard for safety, Georgia law permits punitive damages under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1 to punish the wrongdoer and deter similar conduct.

Trucking companies carry insurance policies with limits that are significantly higher than standard auto policies — often $1 million or more. Roden Law has the experience and resources to litigate against major trucking companies and their national insurers to pursue every dollar of available coverage.

Why Savannah Truck Accident Victims Choose Roden Law

Attorney Eric Roden and the Roden Law team have built a track record of results that speaks for itself. With more than $300 million recovered for injured clients, 5,000+ cases handled, and a 4.9-star average client rating, the firm has established itself as one of the leading personal injury practices in Georgia and South Carolina.

What sets Roden Law apart in truck accident litigation is a combination of resources, preparation, and willingness to go to trial. Trucking companies and their insurers know which law firms will accept a lowball settlement and which firms will take the case to a Chatham County jury. Roden Law has earned a reputation as a firm that prepares every case for trial — and that reputation produces better results for clients at every stage of the process.

The firm operates on a contingency fee basis, meaning clients pay nothing upfront and owe no attorney fees unless Roden Law secures a recovery. With a local office in Savannah, the team is accessible, responsive, and deeply familiar with the courts, roads, and trucking patterns of Chatham County and Southeast Georgia.

Contact Roden Law's Savannah Truck Accident Team

Roden Law is a leading personal injury firm serving Charleston and the surrounding tri-county area, with a 4.9-star average client rating and more than $300 million recovered for injured clients. You work directly with your attorney — not a rotating desk of case managers — from your first call through settlement or verdict. Call (843) 790-8999 for a free, confidential case review.

  • In South Carolina you generally have 3 years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) — miss it and your claim is usually barred.
  • South Carolina uses modified comparative negligence: you can recover as long as you are not more than 50% at fault, though your award is reduced by your share (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.).

Personal Injury Cases We Handle in Charleston

Roden Law handles the full range of serious injury claims for Charleston-area clients, from routine collisions to catastrophic, life-altering injuries. Our busiest area is motor-vehicle crashes, and our Charleston attorneys represent injured people in every major practice area:

  • Charleston car accident lawyers — if you were hurt in a wreck on I-26, the Crosstown, or the Ravenel Bridge, start with our dedicated car accident team, who recover compensation for injured drivers, passengers, and pedestrians across the peninsula and the islands.
  • Truck and 18-wheeler accidents — port-bound tractor-trailers and interstate freight crashes.
  • Motorcycle accidents — riders hurt by inattentive drivers on Lowcountry roads.
  • Pedestrian accidents — walkers struck in the dense King and Market Street grid.
  • Premises liability and slip and fall — injuries on unsafe commercial and rental property.
  • Dog bites — attacks governed by South Carolina's strict-liability statute.
  • Workers' compensation — on-the-job injuries at the port, on job sites, and in warehouses.
  • Maritime and Jones Act injuries — longshore, dockworker, and vessel-crew claims tied to the Port of Charleston.
  • Wrongful death — claims brought by a family after a fatal accident.
  • Golf cart and low-speed-vehicle accidents — a growing problem in island and Goose Creek golf-cart communities.

Whatever the injury, this page sits above our practice-specific pages as a hub — if your situation fits one of the categories above, that dedicated page will have the most detail. This page belongs to our statewide personal injury pillar, which covers the full body of South Carolina injury law.

Why Hire a Local Charleston Personal Injury Attorney

A local attorney matters because a Charleston injury claim is filed, mediated, and tried in local courts under local rules — and knowing those courts, judges, and defense adjusters directly affects what your case is worth. Most Charleston personal injury cases are filed in the Charleston County Court of Common Pleas at 100 Broad Street, part of the Ninth Judicial Circuit, which covers both Charleston and Berkeley counties. Cases arising in Dorchester County are filed in the First Judicial Circuit in St. George.

Charleston's peninsula geography, heavy tourist traffic, and busy working port make its cases uniquely complex, and the local insurance defense bar knows it. What sets Roden Law apart is direct attorney involvement and physical proximity: our King Street office is steps from the courthouse, so filings, hearings, and client meetings happen without delay. The Port of Charleston — one of the busiest container ports on the East Coast — also shapes our caseload, driving maritime, longshore, and heavy-truck claims that a general practitioner rarely handles.

South Carolina Personal Injury Law Essentials

The Deadline

In South Carolina, you generally have three years from the date of your injury to file a personal injury lawsuit (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). If you miss that window, the court will almost always dismiss your case no matter how strong it is, so the deadline is the single most important date in your claim.

The Fault Rule

South Carolina follows modified comparative negligence: you can still recover damages as long as you are not more than 50% at fault for the accident, but your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault, and at 51% or greater you recover nothing (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Insurers exploit this rule aggressively — shifting even a little blame onto you directly lowers what they must pay — which is why early, independent investigation matters.

Who Can File a Wrongful Death Claim

In South Carolina, a wrongful death action must be brought by the personal representative of the deceased person's estate, not directly by grieving family members (S.C. Code § 15-51-20). The recovery is then distributed to the statutory beneficiaries.

Graeham C. Gillin, a South Carolina–licensed partner at the firm, points out that South Carolina's three-year deadline is not a reason to wait: physical evidence from a Charleston crash or fall scene disappears within weeks, surveillance footage is overwritten, and witnesses move on, so the cases that recover the most are almost always the ones investigated early.

Charleston's Most Dangerous Roads and Injury Hotspots

Charleston's most serious injury crashes concentrate on a handful of high-volume corridors where interstate speed, tourist congestion, and bridge geometry collide — a map of where our clients are most often hurt:

  • US-17 Crosstown (Septima P. Clark Parkway)
  • Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge to Mount Pleasant
  • I-26 and I-526 corridors — especially the high-crash I-26/I-526 interchange just west of the peninsula, which produces many of the Lowcountry's most catastrophic wrecks
  • King and Market Street — the dense downtown tourist grid
  • Savannah Highway (US-17) through West Ashley
  • Ashley River Road (SC-61)
  • Rivers Avenue up into North Charleston

According to South Carolina Department of Public Safety data, the state's most severe collisions cluster on exactly these interstate and primary US-route corridors that ring Charleston. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, South Carolina has for years ranked among the states with the highest traffic-death rates per mile driven, a pattern that makes the Lowcountry's tourist-heavy roads especially dangerous.

When those crashes turn catastrophic, serious-injury patients from peninsula collisions are routed to MUSC Health (171 Ashley Avenue) — the Lowcountry's only Level I trauma center. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, motor-vehicle crashes remain a leading cause of injury death and long-term disability in the United States, which is why traumatic brain, spinal-cord, and orthopedic injuries drive so many of the high-value claims we handle.

Compensation Available in a Charleston Personal Injury Claim

You can recover both economic and non-economic damages, and in ordinary injury cases South Carolina places no statutory cap on pain-and-suffering awards:

  • Economic damages — past and future medical bills, lost wages, loss of future earning capacity, and property damage.
  • Non-economic damages — pain and suffering, disfigurement, loss of enjoyment of life, and emotional distress.
  • Punitive damages — may be available in cases involving especially reckless conduct.

According to South Carolina Department of Insurance rules, the state's minimum auto-liability limits are just $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident — often far below what a serious injury actually costs. That gap is why uninsured and underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage matters so much: when the at-fault driver's policy runs out, stacking your own UM/UIM coverage is frequently the difference between a partial and a full recovery. We investigate every available policy so no source of compensation is left on the table.

What to Do After an Injury in Charleston

The single most important step after any serious injury is to get medical care immediately and document everything — because both your health and your claim depend on an early, complete record. Follow these steps:

  1. Get medical attention right away. Even injuries that seem minor — concussions, internal injuries, soft-tissue damage — may not show symptoms for hours or days. A prompt exam protects your health and creates the record insurers respect.
  2. Report the incident and get the official record. For a crash, South Carolina law requires an accident report when there are injuries or significant property damage; request a copy. For a fall or premises injury, notify the property owner or manager and ask that an incident report be created.
  3. Document the scene. Photograph vehicles, hazards, injuries, and conditions. Get names and contact information for every witness before they leave.
  4. Do not give a recorded statement to the other insurer. Adjusters use early statements to shift blame under South Carolina's comparative-negligence rule.
  5. Keep every bill and record. Save medical records, receipts, and proof of missed work.
  6. Call a Charleston personal injury lawyer. The sooner counsel begins investigating, the more evidence is preserved. Reach Roden Law at (843) 790-8999.
